faq.a: Growth plates are thin layers of cartilage near the ends of long bones in children and teenagers. They are where new bone is made, so the bones can grow longer.
Cartilage cells in the growth plate divide and swell, pushing the bone end outwards. The older cartilage behind them is hardened with minerals and replaced by bone, adding length to the shaft.

faq.q: How does cartilage turn into bone?
faq.a: Minerals, mostly calcium phosphate, are laid into the old cartilage, which hardens it. Blood vessels grow in, and bone-building cells called osteoblasts replace the cartilage with real bone.

faq.q: Why do growth plates show up on X-rays?
faq.a: Cartilage lets X-rays through more easily than hard bone, so growth plates look like dark lines across the ends of a child's bones. Doctors can estimate age from them.
asks: Why are there lines on a child's X-ray?
Can an X-ray show how old you are?

faq.a: Growth plates close in the late teens to early twenties, usually earlier in girls than boys. Once closed, the bone cannot grow any longer.
asks: At what age do bones stop growing?

facts: Growth plates are also called epiphyseal plates.
Most growth plates close between about 14 and 19 years old, usually earlier in girls than in boys.
